header.title_plain: Not all muscle growth is equal: for strength and power, grow the fast fibres with heavy loads, not everything with high reps

citation.authors: Travis SK, Ishida A, Taber CB, Fry AC, Stone MH

header.evidence_type: Narrative review / position paper from a strength-and-conditioning research group. Much of the mechanistic content is theoretical.

confidence.why: A coherent argument with real supporting data, but one school of thought; the authors acknowledge disagreement in the field.

practical_relevance.why: Bears on how to program hypertrophy phases for athletes.

header.author_stance: one strength-and-conditioning research group with a stated position; explicitly disagrees with Loenneke's group on size vs strength

review.claim: "Hypertrophy" is not one thing. Bodybuilders and strength athletes can have similar muscle size but very different strength, because which fibres grew and what grew inside them differ. For strength and power, the goal should be optimal rather than maximal hypertrophy: grow type II fibres preferentially (raise the type II : type I size ratio), grow contractile protein rather than non-contractile cell volume, grow the regions of muscles that the competition lift uses, and sequence hypertrophy → strength → power so each phase sets up the next.

evidence_cited.numbers: p70S6K activation correlated with gains in fat-free mass (r = 0.81–0.89), squat 1RM (r = 0.84), type II fibre size (r = 0.82)
high load → type II growth; low load → relatively more type I

evidence_cited.finding: Strength athletes have bigger fast fibres than bodybuilders
evidence_cited.numbers: ~20% greater type II fibre area in powerlifters/weightlifters; type II fibres up to twice the size of type I vs bodybuilders' more even profile

evidence_cited.source: Bjørnsen 2019, Norwegian powerlifters, blood-flow restriction at ~30% 1RM
evidence_cited.numbers: type I +12%, type II +4%; front squat improved (authors attribute partly to novelty)
r = 0.63–0.91 between muscle size and squat/bench/deadlift in national powerlifters
theoretical pennation-angle limit ~30°; a world-champion raw powerlifter measured 33° (477.5 kg squat)
6 weeks of high-volume training: growth mostly sarcoplasmic, with lower actin/myosin concentration
non-failure group showed greater type II hypertrophy and performance than failure group
full squats produced greater growth across more muscles than half squats over 10 weeks
~60% 1RM for whole-muscle growth; ≥80% to target high-threshold motor units; ≥10 reps/set for ~6 weeks may raise AMPK signalling that interferes with type II growth

recommendations_made: Hypertrophy phase for strength/power athletes: 80–95% 1RM, ~5 reps/set, not to failure.
Use full range of motion and competition-specific exercises.
Precede with 2–4 weeks of general hypertrophy/strength-endurance to prime the process.
review.untested_or_contested: Whether size and strength are "completely separate" (they argue no; Loenneke's group argues yes). Fibre-type shift findings are often misclassified. Sarcoplasmic hypertrophy remains controversial. The load thresholds are "theoretical." They call for studies combining ultrasound, biopsy and 1RM testing.

layer2.what_it_means: This is the case for lifting heavy even when the goal is size, if the size is meant to serve strength or power. The supporting facts are solid: heavy loads preferentially grow fast-twitch fibres, strength athletes carry bigger fast fibres than bodybuilders of similar overall size, going to failure doesn't improve fast-fibre growth, and full-depth squats grow more muscle than half squats. For a coach, the practical shape is a hypertrophy block built on 5-ish reps at 80–95% rather than 10–15 reps at 65%, with full range of motion and reps in reserve, followed by strength and power blocks that cash in the new tissue.
layer2.what_it_doesnt_mean: It doesn't say high-rep training is useless — it's the better route to type I growth and general muscle mass, and the authors themselves recommend 2–4 weeks of it first. The molecular story (mTOR, AMPK, myostatin, miRNA) is largely reasoning from mechanism, not from training outcomes; the paper is explicit that the load thresholds are theoretical. It's written by one research group with a known position, and some of its evidence is elite-athlete observation and single-case data. For general-population members chasing size and health, most of this is beside the point.

translation: Strength/power hypertrophy block: 80–95% 1RM, ~5 reps per set, stop short of failure, full depth, lifts that look like the sport.
Light, high-rep work grows slow-twitch fibres; heavy work grows fast-twitch.
Full squats beat half squats for muscle growth (10 weeks).

glossary_candidates.definition: Growth of the force-producing filaments vs growth of the fluid and non-contractile contents of the fibre; both make muscle bigger, only the first makes it proportionally stronger.

glossary_candidates.term: Type II : type I size ratio
glossary_candidates.definition: How much bigger fast fibres are than slow ones; higher in strength and power athletes.
The angle fibres sit at relative to the line of pull; increases with hypertrophy and raises force at some cost to speed.
More in parallel = more force; more in series = more speed and range.
Two opposing cell signals: mTOR drives growth; AMPK responds to endurance-type stress and can dampen it.
Ordering training blocks so each one sets up the next (e.g. hypertrophy → strength → power).
Continuing a set until no more reps are possible.
Growth concentrated in one part of a muscle, depending on the exercise and range of motion.

charts.title: Load → which fibres grow
charts.units: x = load, % 1RM (thresholds as printed); y = 1 if the authors say this fibre type is emphasised at that load, 0 if not — a category, not a measurement
charts.note: schematic — not measured data. <60% 1RM → type I; 60–80% → mixed; ≥80% → type II. Thresholds are labelled theoretical by the authors; y values are illustrative only.
